feed.title: Cost-backed Sybil resistance for self-issued identifiers

entry.title: Cost-backed Sybil resistance for self-issued identifiers
entry.summary:
Open systems commonly issue identifiers such as public keys with virtually no associated resource cost, resulting in a situation where the incremental expense of generating additional identifiers is negligible. This economic structure places the burden of filtering, storage, and abuse management on those who accept these identifiers, rather than on those who produce them. The only practical limitation on volume arises from the capacity of the processing parties, not from any inherent barrier to production. Conventional methods attempt to address this by introducing gating mechanisms before issuance, increasing the effort required for bulk generation. However, these gates often rely on external factors or third-party intervention, introducing friction that impacts legitimate users while failing to ensure lasting resource commitment from bulk producers. Additionally, such gates remain vulnerable to exploitation and denial-of-service attacks.
A novel approach proposes embedding the resource cost directly into the identifier itself, bypassing the need for a centralized issuer or external gatekeeping. The Satoshi Hike 2.3 specification exemplifies this method by requiring the producer to maintain a substantial memory allocation—specifically, 256 MiB—and to execute a sequence of memory-intensive operations tied to consecutive Bitcoin block headers. The process leaves an evidentiary record attached to the resulting object, effectively binding the resource expenditure and computational effort to the identifier. Bitcoin's blockchain serves as an immutable public timeline, offering a reference for ordering without enforcing or subsidizing the creation process.
Verification is performed independently by measuring the object against the published specification and a portable public index. Structural and cryptographic validations are conducted, supplemented by randomized recomputation of selected segments to confirm alignment with the prescribed construction. Success in verification demonstrates adherence to the protocol but does not definitively guarantee that the evidence could not be inexpensively replicated under adversarial conditions. The fundamental challenge remains to determine whether this design imposes sufficiently high marginal costs on self-issued objects to deter abuse, particularly in scenarios involving strategic adversaries.
The resource commitment entailed by this scheme is intrinsically self-attested, encapsulating both the memory residency and its temporal association with the blockchain reference. This commitment is inseparable from the identifier and travels with it throughout its lifecycle. The specification clearly delineates both the object format and the measurement procedures, leaving acceptance policies and minimum cost thresholds to the discretion of individual recipients. No explicit guidance is provided concerning currency-based cost metrics or operational thresholds for acceptance.
Critical analysis is encouraged regarding several facets of this construction. Key areas for review include the effectiveness of time-memory tradeoffs, susceptibility to precomputation or cross-object reuse in undermining production costs, the role and reliability of Bitcoin header bindings, the asymmetry between production and verification efforts, and comparison to related prior art. The central question is whether this approach can render the creation of additional self-issued objects prohibitively expensive in adversarial contexts, and what types of empirical evidence would suffice to substantiate that claim.
For further details, refer to the [Satoshi Hike 2.3 Specification](https://github.com/groundinglab/pcoc).
